title: Meet the building blocks
subtitle: Roots, prefixes and suffixes
html:
A long medical word becomes easier when you look for familiar pieces. A root carries the central meaning, a prefix modifies it at the beginning, and a suffix adds a condition, process or procedure at the end.

PartJobExample
PrefixModifies location, amount or timingperi- → around
RootNames a structure or central ideacard → heart
SuffixAdds a condition or process-itis → inflammation

Put the pieces together.

peri / card / itis gives a useful starting clue: inflammation around the heart. Its precise meaning is inflammation of the pericardium, the sac surrounding the heart.

Word parts give you a route into meaning. Always connect the literal clue to the precise clinical definition.

title: Find the suffix first
subtitle: A practical way to decode
html:
When a term is unfamiliar, find its ending first. It often tells you whether you are reading about a symptom, a condition, an examination or a procedure.

EndingMeaningExample
-algiaPainArthralgia → joint pain
-itisInflammationArthritis → joint inflammation
-ectomySurgical removalNephrectomy → kidney removal
-scopyVisual examinationBronchoscopy → looking inside airways

Then read the root and any prefix. Hepatomegaly: -megaly means enlargement; hepat means liver. The meaning is enlargement of the liver.

title: The little vowel that connects
subtitle: Combining vowels and forms
html:
A combining vowel helps connect word parts. The most common is o. A root plus its combining vowel is called a combining form: cardi/o, gastr/o or neur/o.

Notice what happens at the join.

Gastr/o/scopy keeps the o before a consonant-starting suffix. Gastr/itis drops it before a vowel-starting suffix.

Between two roots the combining vowel is often retained, even if the next root begins with a vowel: oste/o/arthr/itis.

A combining vowel links the parts; it does not add a separate clinical meaning. These are useful patterns, with exceptions.

title: A small prefix, a big difference
subtitle: Compare, contrast and remember
html:
Prefixes often come in memorable contrasts. Learn each pair together so the difference becomes easier to spot.

PairMeaningClinical language
hyper- / hypo-Above or excessive / below or deficientHyperglycaemia / hypoglycaemia
tachy- / brady-Fast / slowTachycardia / bradycardia
endo- / peri-Within / aroundEndocarditis / pericarditis
pre- / post-Before / afterPrenatal / postnatal

Take an extra moment with similar-looking terms. Changing just one prefix can reverse the meaning of an observation.

title: Spelling travels. Meaning stays.
subtitle: AU/NZ and US conventions
html:
This studio follows the Australian/New Zealand spelling used in the reference book. You will also meet US spellings in journals, software and clinical resources.

AU/NZUS
anaemiaanemia
haematuriahematuria
dyspnoeadyspnea
leucocyteleukocyte

Plurals can change the ending.

Vertebra → vertebrae. Bronchus → bronchi. Diagnosis → diagnoses. Metastasis → metastases. Do not assume every medical plural is formed by adding s.

Search in the term library recognises the common variants provided for each entry.

title: Meaning lives in context
subtitle: When literal decoding is not enough
html:
Decoding is a starting point. Some word elements have more than one meaning, and some established clinical definitions go beyond their literal parts.

One root, more than one possibility.

Myel/o may refer to bone marrow or the spinal cord. In osteomyelitis, the context is bone and marrow. Cyst/o can mean a bladder, cyst or sac; in cystoscopy it refers to the urinary bladder.

The literal clue is not the final definition.

Anaemia does not mean that a person has no blood. It refers to haemoglobin below the appropriate range. Pericarditis specifies the pericardial sac, rather than any inflammation near the heart.

Use the pieces to form a hypothesis. Use a trusted definition and the clinical context to confirm it.

title: Translate with clarity
subtitle: From clinical term to shared understanding
html:
Good clinical language supports shared understanding. Keep the precise term when it is useful, then add a clear everyday explanation.

Clinical termA clear explanation
DyspnoeaFeeling short of breath
HepatomegalyAn enlarged liver
NephrectomyAn operation to remove all or part of a kidney
SubcutaneousUnder the skin

With abbreviations, check the intended meaning in context. Local policies and specialties may use the same letters differently. Write a term in full when that makes communication clearer.

Make it stick.

Close the explanation, recall the meaning, then check it. Use the flashcards and short practice sets to revisit terms after a gap.
